title: Plastic chopping boards: wash, sanitise, rinse and dry on edge
audience: Cleaners who clean kitchens in residential, short-stay, bond and commercial work, including staff who handle sanitising products for kitchen items.
learningOutcomes: Put a plastic chopping board through the scrape, wash, rinse, sanitise, rinse and dry sequence in the order given.
Use a sanitising product only at the label's dilution and contact time, with the PPE that the label sets.
Store a board so that it drains and dries and does not hold water.
Recognise a board that cannot be cleaned to standard, and take it out of use.

instruction.heading: Why boards get their own steps
instruction.body: A chopping board holds food residue in its knife grooves and its surface, so a quick wipe is not enough. Because the board is used for food, the business's food-safety plan and the rules that apply to food-contact items matter as well as the cleaning method. This lesson covers the cleaning and drying steps for plastic boards as the source sets them out. It does not set food-premises requirements.

instruction.heading: Scrape, wash and rinse first
instruction.body: Scrape heavy debris and soiling into the bin before any water touches the board. Wash the board in a detergent solution made up to the label, using a brush or scrubber to work into the grooves. Rinse it in fresh water to remove the detergent, because detergent left on the board can interfere with a sanitiser. Change the wash water when it is visibly soiled. If residue will not lift with the brush, soak the board briefly in the detergent solution, then scrub again. Do not move on to the sanitising step until the board is visibly free of residue.

instruction.heading: Sanitise at the label's dilution and time
instruction.body: The source soaks plastic boards in a sanitising solution for a time set by the source, and it gives a dilution for its product. Both are historical values for a product named in a 2012 hospital manual. This lesson does not endorse that product and does not use those figures as current instructions. Use only a sanitiser on the business's approved products list, make it up to that product's label, and hold the board in contact for the time the label gives. Contact time is the time the sanitiser needs to work, not the time it takes to wipe. If the label gives no time, stop and check the safety data sheet and the approved method before using it. Never mix this sanitiser with another product in the same container or sink.

instruction.heading: Rinse, dry and store on edge
instruction.body: Rinse the sanitised board in fresh water to remove the sanitiser, then stand it on its edge so that both faces shed water and air out. Laying the board flat traps water in the grooves and underneath, which lets residue and odour build up. Store the dry board on its edge in its allocated place, away from chemical containers. A board that is still damp should not be put away.

instruction.heading: Working safely with the sanitiser
instruction.body: Sanitising is a chemical-hazard step. Wear the gloves and any eye protection the approved product's label lists, and make up the solution where there is adequate ventilation. The source warns against inhaling sprayed product and asks for ventilation, and those points carry over to any sprayed product. Rinse and dry your hands after use, and protect the skin if contact is prolonged. Keep the sanitiser container closed when it is not in use, and keep it labelled with the product name and dilution. If a product gets into your eyes or onto your skin, follow the first aid steps on the label and the safety data sheet, and report it to your supervisor at once.

instruction.heading: Boards that must come out of use
instruction.body: Take a board out of use when it has deep grooves or cracks that the brush cannot clean, when it has warped, or when a smell does not clear after the full sequence. Report it to the supervisor and have it replaced under the business's equipment process. Do not try to repair a cracked board with tape or filler, and do not keep using a board whose surface has been lost. A board that is out of use is stored apart from the boards in service, so that nobody picks it up by mistake.

procedure: Put on the gloves and any eye protection that the approved sanitiser label lists, before you open the sanitiser container.
Scrape heavy debris into the bin, then wash the board in detergent made up to its label, working the brush into the grooves.
Rinse the board in fresh water, and change the wash water if it is visibly soiled.
Make up the sanitiser at the approved product's label dilution, and hold the board in contact for the label's time.
Rinse the board in fresh water to remove the sanitiser, then stand it on its edge so both faces shed water and dry out.
Check the board for grooves, cracks or odour. Store it dry on its edge in its allocated place, or take it out of use and report it.

workedExamples.situation: A residential kitchen after a family dinner. A plastic board has heavy residue in its grooves and a strong smell.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which steps come first, and what do you do if the smell remains?
workedExamples.reasoning: Scrape the residue into the bin, wash with a brush in detergent, rinse, then sanitise at the approved label dilution and contact time. Stand the board on its edge to dry. If the smell remains after the full sequence, take the board out of use and report it, because the grooves may be holding residue that the method cannot clear.

workedExamples.situation: A short-stay turnover. The sanitiser bottle runs out, and you consider topping it up with the detergent left in the other bottle.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not mix products, and do not top up a sanitiser with a detergent. Make up a fresh batch from the approved product at the label dilution, label the container, and record the batch under the business's product process. Mixing products can create a hazard, and the result cannot be relied on.

workedExamples.situation: A commercial kitchen has a board with a deep crack. A cook asks you to put it back with the sound boards so that it can be used later.
workedExamples.reasoning: Take the board out of use, because the crack holds residue that the sanitising sequence cannot clear. Report it to the supervisor for replacement under the business's equipment process, and store it apart from the boards in service.

equipmentAndPpe: Gloves and eye protection that the approved sanitiser label lists
Plastic chopping boards, a brush or scraper, and a clean container for detergent
Detergent and sanitiser from the approved products list, with the label and the safety data sheet available
Measuring device for the dilution the label gives
Container labelled with the product name and dilution
Drying space where boards can stand on their edge

commonErrors.error: Laying a board flat to dry.
commonErrors.prevention: Stand it on its edge so that both faces drain and dry.

commonErrors.error: Topping up a sanitiser with a different product.
commonErrors.prevention: Never mix products. Make up a fresh batch from the approved product at the label dilution.

commonErrors.error: Treating the sanitiser contact time as the time it takes to wipe.
commonErrors.prevention: Hold the board in contact for the label's time, then rinse.

commonErrors.error: Keeping a board with a deep crack in service.
commonErrors.prevention: Take it out of use, store it apart, and report it for replacement.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Sanitising is a chemical-hazard step. Dilution, PPE, ventilation and first aid are set by the product label, the safety data sheet and the business procedure.
This lesson does not confirm compliance with any food rule.
The source's soak time, its dilution and its product name are historical 2012 hospital values. They are not used as current instructions, and the contact time must come from the current label.

qualityStandard: Each board is scraped, washed, rinsed, sanitised at the label's dilution and contact time, rinsed, and dried on edge, in that order.
No board is stored damp, stored flat, or stored with visible residue.
Sanitiser is made up only from an approved product at the label dilution, and it is never mixed with another product.
A worn or damaged board is taken out of use and reported.
documentationEvidence: Record of the sanitiser product, batch, dilution and contact time used on each shift.
Report of any board taken out of use, with the reason.
summary: Scrape, wash and rinse before sanitising.
Sanitise at the label's dilution and contact time, with an approved product and the PPE the label sets.
Rinse, then stand the board on its edge so both faces shed water and dry out.
Take out of use any board that cannot be cleaned, and report it.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is a board stood on its edge after rinsing?
options: So that dust settles on the top face where it is easy to see
So that both faces drain and dry, and water does not sit in the grooves
So that the sanitiser runs off faster before the next use

knowledgeChecks.question: The sanitiser runs out during a turnover. What is the correct action?
options: Top it up with the detergent that is left, since it is also a sanitiser
Make up a fresh batch from the approved product at the label dilution, and label it
Use the sanitiser at double strength because the board looks very dirty

knowledgeChecks.question: A plastic board has a deep crack and still smells after the full sequence. What should you do?
options: Take it out of use and report it for replacement
Store it on its edge with the sound boards for the next job
Cover the crack with tape and keep using it
